---
title: "Style guide"
---

Every team has conventions a linter can't express, like banning `print()` in committed code, `import *`, and bare `except:`. captain-hook ships *no* rules of its own. You write the cross-language shape checks as [ast-grep](https://ast-grep.github.io) patterns with `ast_grep_rule()`, the Python-specific ones as `StyleRule` subclasses, and hand them all to `styleguide()`, which parses each edited file, runs every rule, and reports only the violations your edit introduced.

<!-- gd-embed: styleguide.py -->

The `styleguide()` call registers one PostToolUse hook that fires after every Python edit or write, skipping test files by default. `ast_grep_rule()` builds a rule from one ast-grep pattern. `NoPrint` is `print($$$)`, which matches a print call however its arguments are spelled and never a string or comment that mentions one. `message` is the text shown, with `{violations}` substituted at fire time, and `label` names each match. `NoNewWildcardImport` uses `ast_grep_diff_rule()` to flag matches present in the new file but absent from the old one, reporting only what the edit *added*. `NoBareExcept` is a plain `StyleRule`. A bare `except:` is `ExceptHandler.type is None`, a Python-AST fact no pattern string expresses, so it matches the tree with a [`matchers`](../guide/styleguide.qmd) expression. That split is the dividing line. Reach for ast-grep on call, literal, and import *shapes*, especially across languages, and a `StyleRule` for Python naming, ordering, and scope. Both kinds register in the same `styleguide(...)` call. The runner renders `label (line N)` and drops any violation whose line you didn't touch, so editing one function never lights up a pre-existing `print()` elsewhere in the file. Pass `block=True` or scope it with `only_if=` to register a second, differently scoped hook. See also [the style guide](../guide/styleguide.qmd) and [the conditions guide](../guide/conditions.qmd) for scoping hooks.
